Document

/DOK-yuh-ment/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Document means a piece of written, printed, or electronic material that provides information or evidence.

The historian found a water-stained document proving the village had traded with foreign sailors as early as the 1600s.

Worked Example

Before boarding, every passenger had to show a travel document — a passport or visa — confirming who they were and where they could go.

The passport is a piece of printed material whose whole job is to provide official information and evidence — identity, citizenship, permission to travel. Providing information or proof is exactly what makes something a document.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

record: A record is a written account of something that happened — the word points at the event it preserves. A document is the piece of written material itself, whatever it contains. A log entry is a record of a voyage; the water-stained page it sits on is a document.

certificate: A certificate is an official paper attesting to one fact — a birth, a marriage, a completed course — and it must be issued by an authority. A document is any piece of written material that provides information or evidence. Every certificate is a document; almost no documents are certificates.

file: A file is a stored collection of papers or data kept together under one label. A document is a single piece of written material inside such a collection. A lawyer pulls the client's file and takes one document out of it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hearsay: unrecorded, secondhand spoken information

rumor: an unverified story passed by word of mouth

Where it sits · how much official weight it carries — note → document → dossier

note vs. document: A note is more casual than a document — a sticky note on the fridge reminds you to buy milk, but it carries no official weight.

dossier vs. document: A dossier is weightier than a single document — investigators compiled an entire dossier of contracts, receipts, and letters on the shell company.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — docu-

Root — docu-: to teach, to show (Latin docere)

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together

Put it together: No prefix here — just docu- (to teach) + -ment (that which results). Latin documentum meant "a lesson, a proof": literally "the thing that teaches." A document is a written thing that teaches or proves something to whoever reads it.

Use the root in a new word: doctrine

Use the root in a new word: doctrine: The court's ruling rested on a legal doctrine — a body of taught principles — developed over two centuries.

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday-to-official

This card teaches the noun. Document also works as a verb — to document something is to record it in detail ("the biologist documented every nest she found"), pronounced with the same stress. On the SAT, the noun sense (a paper or file that provides evidence) is the one you'll meet most.
